newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Vanguard city to give verdict on Russian reforms.
newsitem.headline: Vanguard city to give verdict on Russian reforms.

text.p: Five years after becoming the cradle of Russian reform, the city of Nizhny Novgorod on the Volga gives its verdict on Sunday in a vote which may also help decide who will succeed Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin.

The name that sounds loudest in the campaign for governor of Nizhny Novgorod belongs to neither of the leading candidates. It is Boris Nemtsov, the whiz-kid former governor who put the depressed region on the international investment map.

Nemtsov, 37, is now one of Russia's two first deputy prime ministers and a strong candidate for the presidency. But to win that prize, much depends on how the country's second big reform push since the collapse of communism goes down with the people.

"It is a matter of great importance to me who wins in my native Nizhny Novgorod region," Nemtsov said this week. Yeltsin called the young reformer into the Russian cabinet in March, forcing Sunday's election for the city governership.
For Nemtsov, and the communists who love to hate him, the election is a crucial litmus test of the radical new government's first 100 days in power.
For some 2.8 million voters, it is a chance to say what they think of being chosen as the guinea pigs for Russia's lurch towards capitalism after 70 years of central planning.
Nemtsov is backing Ivan Sklyarov, the mayor of Nizhny Novogorod and the only serious contender in the five-horse race apart from the Communist Party's Gennady Khodyrev.
Electoral commission consultant Pavel Vakhramov said the first round is likely to be inconclusive, in which case the two top candidates go through to a runoff to be held within 15 days.

In 1992, Western advisers descended on Russia's third largest city with plans to conduct an unprecedented experiment. They proceeded to privatise shops, small businesses, trucks and began reorganising collective farms in the surrounding region.
"Nemtsov played a very big role," said Rafael Golebiowski, representative of the International Finance Corporation, the private sector lending arm of the World Bank which has spearheaded the reforms.
The West approved. Not all local people agreed.
"Nemtsov experimented on us," said taxi driver Vladimir Mosalyev. "He did a lot but people haven't felt the benefits."

Statistics compiled by the Russian-European Centre for Economic Policy rank Nizhny Novgorod fifth in terms of per capita foreign direct investment out of Russia's 89 regions, but only 33rd in terms of domestic investment.

The heavily-industrialised region has relatively low official unemployment and has kept a lid on its fiscal gap, but ranks only average in terms of income per capita and change in industrial output, now almost half its 1990 level.
The figures translate into widespread dissatisfaction from those who have lost out from reforms, dissatisfaction which the communists hope will secure them victory at the polls.
"There is this myth that everyone here lives well because of the reforms," said Khodyrev. "If I win it will explode the myth," the Communist candidate told Reuters.

Scenting victory, Russian Communist party leader Gennady Zyuganov has trekked down to the region to lend his support. He has been joined by ultra-nationalist Vladimir Zhirinovsky, whose hatred of Nemtsov outdoes that of even the Communists. Nemtsov once baited Zhirinovsky into throwing his orange juice at him in a television debate.

"People of Nizhny Novgorod, it's up to you. Do you want to live the Nemtsov way or like human beings?" the national leftist daily Sovietskaya Rossiya splashed across the front page of a special election edition.

On Monday, Nemtsov hit back, giving a grim description of life under Khodyrev when the region, then known as Gorky, was a secretive centre for the Soviet Union's vast defence industry and long the city of exile for the late Nobel Peace prize laureate, Andrei Sakharov.

"What was Nizhny Novgorod like during the rule of the Communist Khodyrev?" he said at a news conference. "A gloomy, desolate region unknown even to Soviet people, a closed town with potholed streets...and people with downcast faces."
